Secretaries bridge policy intent with administrative execution: Shri Shashi Ranjan Kumar, Secretary, UPSC
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                16 NOV 2026 5:09PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) today hosted a one-day Workshop for Secretaries of State Public Service Commissions at Dholpur House, New Delhi. The workshop brought together the officers who run the day-to-day machinery of recruitment in the States. Secretaries, Joint Secretaries and senior officers of State Commissions from across the country gathered to identify operational bottlenecks, share proven solutions, and work towards harmonising administrative standards nationwide.
Organised in pursuance of a decision of the 25th National Conference of Chairpersons of State Public Service Commissions, held in Bengaluru in January 2025, the workshop gives the Secretaries, the operating arm of every Commission, a national platform of their own. It comes at a time when the Commissions face the twin task of conducting large-scale examinations securely and using technology to stay ahead of those who try to misuse it.
Addressing the gathering, Dr. Ajay Kumar, Chairman, UPSC, said, "At the UPSC centenary celebrations, the Hon'ble Prime Minister emphasised the importance of sharing best practices among Public Service Commissions, and this workshop is a realisation of that vision. This is a time of reform and innovation, and technology has a big part to play in it. When people use technology to beat the system, the only way is to use more technology to keep a check on them, so that the system remains fair and transparent and the integrity of the examination process is upheld." He also outlined recent initiatives of the Commission, including AI-enabled face authentication of candidates at examination venues, the Universal Registration Number for applicants, digitisation of Departmental Promotion Committee proposals and computerised randomisation of interview boards.
Welcoming the participants, Shri Shashi Ranjan Kumar, Secretary, UPSC, said, "This is not a workshop where we teach and you learn. It is a gathering of colleagues who perform the same responsibilities in different circumstances, under the same constitutional obligations. While Chairpersons and Members shape the vision, it is our duty as Secretaries to ensure that operational mechanisms are robust, legally sound, fair and technologically modern. We bridge policy intent with administrative execution." He noted that many State Commissions have developed effective solutions in areas such as digital processing of applications, conduct of examinations in regional languages and grievance redressal, and urged participants to pool these into a shared repository of best practices. He added that, depending on the feedback, the workshop could become an annual feature.
Outlining the focus of the working sessions, the UPSC Secretary said, "The presentations rest on four pillars of our shared work: secure examinations that preserve public trust, transparent selection, recruitment rules that keep pace with modern job profiles, and disciplinary advice that balances administrative firmness with natural justice."
Following the inaugural session, the workshop moved into four working sessions in which the Commission's branches dealing with examinations, recruitment, recruitment rules, and disciplinary and appeal cases presented their procedures and practices, each followed by an open discussion with the participating officers. The programme concluded with a vote of thanks and a visit to the UPSC Museum.

title: Forest Rights Act
subtitle: Recognising Rights, Securing Livelihoods
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                16 NOV 2026 1:39PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Forest Rights Act (FRA), 2006 recognises the rights of Scheduled Tribes and other traditional forest dwellers on forest land. Individual and community rights are recognised through titles which are official documents that record forest rights. Entering titles into revenue records makes it easier for the owners to get benefits under PM-KISAN and other agriculture, fisheries and livelihood schemes. As on 31 August 2026,
25.42 lakh
titles had been distributed, covering nearly
238 lakh
acres of land. The Ministry launched
National FRA Digital Platform
during the Janjatiya Gaurav Pakhwada. This will bring the claims process, from submission to the Gram Sabha to getting digitally signed titles, on a single platform.
Introduction
For generations, forest-dwelling communities have lived in and depended on forests for their homes and livelihood. Yet the rights of many of them over the land they used went unrecorded when State forests were consolidated during the colonial period and after independence. The Forest Rights Act, 2006 recognises these rights for forest-dwelling Scheduled Tribes and other traditional forest dwellers. It gives legal recognition to both individual and collective rights of these communities on forest land. The Act and its Rules provide for issuing titles to land and entering them in revenue records. The Act received the President’s assent on 29 December 2006 and came into force on 31 December 2007.
The objectives of the Act are:
To recognise forest rights that could not be recorded earlier.
To give forest-dwelling Scheduled Tribes and other traditional forest dwellers secure rights to their land (land tenure), livelihood and food security.
To strengthen forest conservation by giving forest rights holders the responsibility and authority to use forests sustainably and to conserve biodiversity and ecological balance.
The Ministry of Tribal Affairs is the nodal agency for the Act. State Governments and Union Territory Administrations implement it. The Act is being implemented in 20 States and one Union Territory, Jammu and Kashmir.
What is a Forest Rights Title?
A title is the official document that records a forest right. It shows who holds the right, in which village, and over which land or forest, with its boundaries. Three district officers sign it for the State Government: the Divisional Forest Officer, the District Tribal Welfare Officer and the District Collector. The holder gets a certified copy. For a community title, the Gram Sabha (the village assembly) gets it. A title passes to the holder’s heirs. It cannot be sold or transferred.

Comprehensive guidelines on implementing the Act were issued to State Governments and Union Territory Administrations.

A direction to extend the Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi (PM-KISAN) to Forest Right Patta (forest rights title) holders was issued.

Who Can Claim and What the Act Protects
The Act covers two groups. Forest-dwelling Scheduled Tribes are members of Scheduled Tribes who mainly live in forests or forest land and depend on them for their bonafide livelihood needs. Other traditional forest dwellers are those who have mainly lived in forests and depended on them for at least three generations (75 years), before 13 December 2005. Rights apply to forest land occupied before that date. For land held for a home or for cultivation, the right covers only the area actually occupied, up to four hectares.
The rights cover forest land of every kind, including reserved and protected forests, Sanctuaries and National Parks.
No member of either group can be evicted or removed from the forest land they occupy until the recognition and verification of their rights is complete.
The Central Government provides for small areas of forest land, each under one hectare, to be used for government facilities when the Gram Sabha recommends it. These facilities include schools, hospitals, anganwadis, fair price shops, drinking water, minor irrigation canals, roads and community centres.
Kinds of Rights and Titles
Three kinds of title
Individual title:
for the land a family lives on or farms, up to four hectares. A married couple gets it in both their names (in the case of a single-headed household, it is registered in the name of the single head of the household).
Community forest rights title:
for what a village uses together, such as grazing, fishing, water bodies and minor forest produce. The community holds the title. Any conditions are written on it.
Community forest resource title:
gives the Gram Sabha or community the right to protect, regenerate, conserve and manage the forest within its customary boundary. This is the forest the village has traditionally had access to.
Forest dwellers own the minor forest produce they have traditionally collected, such as bamboo, honey, lac, tendu leaves and medicinal plants. They may collect, use and dispose of it.
Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups have rights over their habitat, the area they have customarily lived in, including in reserved and protected forests. The Ministry issued guidelines on Habitat Rights on 5 January 2026. Habitat rights have been granted to 11 Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups in three States: Odisha, Chhattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh.
How a Claim Is Decided
The Gram Sabha starts the process. It is the assembly of all adult members of a village, with the full and unrestricted participation of women. The Gram Sabha elects a Forest Rights Committee of ten to fifteen members. This committee helps it receive and verify claims. At least two-thirds of the committee’s members are from Scheduled Tribes, and at least one-third are women. The Gram Sabha receives claims, verifies them and maps the land. It then passes a resolution. This resolution goes to the Sub-Divisional Level Committee (SDLC). The Act also empowers forest rights holders and the Gram Sabha to protect wildlife, forests, biodiversity and water sources.
The SDLC examines the resolution and prepares the record of forest rights (the list of rights proposed for recognition). It sends this to the District Level Committee (DLC). The DLC’s decision is final and binding. Each of these committees includes officers of the State’s Revenue, Forest and Tribal Affairs departments. It also includes three members of Panchayati Raj Institutions, two of whom are Scheduled Tribe members and at least one of whom is a woman.
A person who disagrees with a Gram Sabha resolution or an SDLC decision can petition the next committee within 60 days. Under the Forest Rights Rules, the committee may allow up to 30 more days. The Ministry has stressed that every rejection must come with an order giving reasons. This order must be sent to the claimant so that the right of appeal is kept.
Once titles are issued, the rights are entered in revenue and forest records. The Forest Rights Rules have required this since 2008, and a 2012 amendment set a time limit of three months.
The State Level Monitoring Committee monitors the process. It is chaired by the Chief Secretary and is to meet at least once in three months.
Progress So Far
As on 31 August 2026, about 54 lakh claims had been received and 43.56 lakh (80.64%) had been disposed of, and 25.42 lakh titles had been distributed, covering nearly 238 lakh acres.
The latest State-wise data, as on 31 August 2026, shows 24.18 lakh individual and 1.24 lakh community titles.

Support for the States
States and Union Territories send Monthly Progress Reports on claims, titles and rejections, and the Ministry compiles them.
The Ministry has demonstrated a national FRA Portal and an FRA mobile app to digitise and map FRA records. It has urged States to link their records with the Portal.
The Ministry launched the National FRA Digital Platform during Janjatiya Gaurav Pakhwada (1 to 15 November 2026): the fortnight of programmes observed across the country. The Platform will bring the whole claims process onto one system, from Gram Sabha submission to digitally signed titles.
District Collectors and District Magistrates have been advised to dispose of pending claims on time. The Ministry also holds regular review meetings with State Tribal Welfare Departments. Grievances received by the Ministry are sent to the States and Union Territories concerned for action.
Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan (DA-JGUA)
Under the scheme, the Ministry funds FRA cells at State and district levels for two years. These cells help settle pending claims and help the SDLC and DLC meet on time. Support also covers State FRA portals, including digital mapping of land records, servers, software and security audits. Additionally, under the Support to Tribal Research Institutes scheme, the Ministry provides ₹25 lakh per State for mapping of potential forest area.
Under DA-JGUA
,
the Ministry provides ₹15 lakh for each Community Forest Resource Management Plan, the plan for protecting and managing a village’s community forest, prepared by a Gram Sabha. It also provides ₹1 lakh for technical support. A joint communication of the Ministry of Tribal Affairs and the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, dated 27 July 2026, allows these plans to be aligned with Forest Department Working Plans. These are the Forest Department’s own plans for managing forests. The Gram Sabha’s authority remains central.
Free courses on the Forest Rights Act are available on iGOT, the online learning platform of Mission Karmayogi. States are also organizing legal literacy camps on forest rights.
In Maharashtra, a Government Resolution of 10 July 2026 provides separate village forms, 7E (record of rights into revenue records) and 12E (crop register), for individual forest rights holders. These forms help them obtain crop loans, Kisan Credit Cards, crop insurance and Direct Benefit Transfer.
Andhra Pradesh links its Giribhumi FRA portal with the State’s revenue and banking systems. Telangana’s online title system is integrated with the BhuBharathi revenue portal.
In September and October 2026, the Ministry held three Regional Review Conferences, in Bengaluru, Kolkata and Srinagar, with 19 States and the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir. They reviewed progress and called for time-bound action plans.
Conclusion
The Forest Rights Act, 2006, gives forest-dwelling communities the legal basis to claim rights over the forests they have long lived in and protected. With 25.42 lakh titles distributed over nearly 238 lakh acres, the focus now is on three things: entering recognised rights in revenue and forest records, linking forest rights holders to livelihood schemes, and supporting Gram Sabhas to manage community forest resources.

title: Kutch Earthquake 2001
subtitle: Leading Through Crisis, Rebuilding Lives, Building Resilience
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                16 NOV 2026 11:34AM by PIB Delhi
content:
Nobody in Gujarat had rehearsed for this, yet leadership rose to the moment. Local officers decided on the spot, even as networks failed. The Centre released Rs. 500 crore that same day. Within two weeks, a new authority, chaired by the Chief Minister, took charge of recovery. Villagers shaped decisions, and families led the rebuilding of their own homes. District Judges, serving as ombudsmen, gave complaints a fair hearing. In October 2001, the Chief Minister raised the momentum further. Eleven senior Secretaries spent weekends in the worst-hit talukas, reporting to him every Monday. Their goal: visible progress by the first anniversary. By 2004, about 1.87 lakh homes stood rebuilt. Kutch proved that humility, urgency and trust can rebuild a region.
A Morning That Changed Gujarat
On the morning of 26 January 2001 at 8:46 a.m., an earthquake of magnitude 6.9 struck Gujarat, with its epicentre in Kutch. This earthquake presented an unprecedented test of leadership, governance and institutional resilience. It affected about 7,633 villages in 181 talukas, which are administrative sub-divisions of a district
.
Nearly one crore people were affected across these places, and 13,805 lives were lost, including 12,221 in Kutch. About 1.67 lakh people were injured, and the scale of human suffering was immense across the region.
More than two lakh houses were destroyed and about nine lakhs were damaged, leaving countless families without shelter. Livelihoods were hit just as hard, as over 10,000 small and medium industrial units suspended production. About 50,000 artisans also lost their livelihoods, adding an economic crisis to the human tragedy of the day. Gujarat had emergency plans for cyclones and floods, but it did not have a plan specific to earthquakes.
Yet, the tragedy also demanded decisive leadership, with swift decisions, coordinated action and a vision that went beyond immediate relief to rebuilding a safer and more resilient Gujarat.
The First Hours: Acting Before Certainty
On 26 January, the Director of Relief reached the State Control Room at Gandhinagar and began coordinating the response. Communication soon became a major challenge, as landline and mobile networks in the capital region failed within an hour
. Satellite phones and the police wireless
remained the principal means of communication in the hours that followed.
In Bhuj, the Superintendent of Police took charge of search and rescue, and the Collector led relief and supply. A
medical camp was set up
on open ground within about two hours, bringing care to the injured. After a request to the Brigadier, an
Army platoon was deployed
, and
police families started a community kitchen
. The Government of India acted the same day, as the
National Crisis Management Committee met under the Prime Minister
.
Rs. 500 crore was sanctioned for immediate relief
, which allowed urgent work to begin without delay. Armed forces and paramilitary forces joined the rescue effort, and relief supplies were airlifted to the region.
An Institution for the Mission: The Making of State Disaster Management Authority
As the first phase of relief progressed, attention turned to the larger task of rehabilitation and reconstruction. On 8 February 2001, the Government of Gujarat constituted the
Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority
, known as GSDMA.
It was set up through a Government Resolution with a mandate to oversee re-building. The model was not entirely new, as it drew on the Orissa State Disaster Management Authority. That body was created by the State Government after the 1999 super cyclone to lead recovery. The Government of India had suggested that Gujarat set up a similar body of its own.
At first, GSDMA was a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, and it became an authority established by law. This change came through the Gujarat State Disaster Management Act, 2003, which gave the Authority a firm legal basis.
The Governing Body set policy and guidelines, and it comprised the Chief Minister as Chairman, senior Ministers and senior officers. On 10 February 2001, the Governing Body adopted an initial framework that
involved public participation i.e., villagers in key decisions
.
Village Committees and Gram Sabhas
were to take part in decisions on relocation of severely damaged villages. At the national level, the Government of India constituted a National Committee on Disaster Management on 13 February 2001. This step followed an all-party meeting convened by the Prime Minister in the days after the earthquake.
Counting the Cost: Funding the Recovery
Rebuilding a region on this scale needed large funds, and the first step was to estimate the cost.
Joint assessments by the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank placed the damage at Rs. 9,909 crore
.
They estimated the cost of reconstruction at about Rs. 10,575 crore
, and both are international lending institutions. The
State Government later placed its own estimate at about Rs. 8,496 crore
, which was lower than the joint estimate. The two institutions had first sanctioned loans of US$ 1 billion (Rs. 100 Crore) and US$ 500 million (Rs. 50 Crore). After review, these loan sanctions were revised to US$ 703 million (Rs. 70.3 crore) and US$ 350 million (Rs. 35 crore) respectively.
The State Government met about 30 per cent of the cost, approximately Rs. 2,603 crore, from its own resources.
The Owner-Driven Approach: Families at the Centre
With funds in view, the Government turned to housing and announced four housing assistance packages on 23 February 2001. The assistance varied by the severity of damage, the seismic risk and the type of settlement.
A fifth package followed on 24 April 2001 for the four worst-affected towns of Kutch: Bhuj, Bhachau, Anjar and Rapar. The reconstruction policy provided for an
owner-driven approach, under which families rebuilt their own houses instead of using contractors
.
The Government gave families financial assistance, technical guidance and safe designs to help them rebuild. Non-governmental organisations and private partners also played a part, building houses in adopted villages under a public-private partnership programme.
Under this programme, each side contributed funds, and money was released in stages as construction progressed. Official documents described the entire programme as reconstruction plus, also known as building back better.
Making It Work on the Ground: Leadership in Implementation
Damage assessment
The first step was to assess the damage, which was graded on a scale from G1 to G5. In this scale
, G1 meant minor damage
and
G5 meant complete destruction or damage beyond repair
. Surveys were undertaken by 2,051 teams comprising a total of 4,592 persons, including 1,794 revenue officers. Each survey team had three members, and the community was involved in the survey process. Families could request a re-survey, and the period for applications was extended to allow this.
Grievance redressal
Complaints were handled by village committees, district committees and the District Judge, who was designated Ombudsman in each district
. An Ombudsman is an official who looks into complaints from the public against the administration. The Ombudsman could receive complaints directly from the public and direct the administration to act on them. By October 2003, the
Ombudsmen had received 47,156 petitions, and about 99 per cent of these had been dealt with
.
Administrative structure
A four-tier structure operated at the State, district, taluka and village levels, with Additional Collectors posted in the worst-affected talukas. In each village, a committee called the
Gram Navrachna Samiti
supervised the reconstruction work in that village.
Its members included the Sarpanch, the elected village head, a woman member, and members of backward castes and minority communities
. The primary school headmaster and a representative of a non-governmental organisation were also part of the committee.
Government departments carried out works, while the Authority, led by Chief Executive Officer Dr P.K. Mishra, coordinated and monitored them. District Collectors served as Joint Chief Executive Officers, and an operational manual was prepared to speed up approval of works.
Assistance and quality arrangements
Assistance was paid to beneficiaries in
instalments,
with an engineer certifying the progress of construction at each stage.
A total of 1,082 material banks supplied cement
and other materials, while nearly
30,000 masons
and
6,200 engineers
were trained.
About 2.6 lakh houses were inspected independently, and reconstructed houses were registered jointly in the names of husband and wife
. New construction incorporated earthquake-resistant and cyclone-resistant features.
Reviewing Progress, Renewing Momentum
By October 2001, a review of progress showed both achievements and problems that still needed attention. A number of families continued to live in tents, and some offices and schools still functioned from temporary buildings.
Urban reconstruction proceeded more slowly than rural reconstruction, as it required plot surveys, road widening and reallocation of land. Water shortages or site-related difficulties were reported in some of the new villages built after the earthquake.
Action was also taken in connection with debris clearance, with disciplinary action against 276 government employees. Cases were also initiated against 738 persons linked to local bodies in the same matter.
Shri Narendra Modi assumed office as Chief Minister in October 2001, and a fresh review of progress followed. After the review, eleven senior Secretaries were assigned to the worst-affected talukas for focused attention. Each Secretary visited the assigned area for three days every weekend until the end of January 2002.
A review meeting chaired by the Chief Minister was held every Monday during this period. The stated objective was to demonstrate progress by the first anniversary of the earthquake on 26 January 2002. Based on field visits and the Secretaries’ suggestions, a number of policy and operational issues were resolved.
As a result of these steps, the pace of reconstruction and rehabilitation increased in the following months.
Homes, Towns and Livelihoods: Progress by 2004
Housing
Repair work was largely completed in the first year, while reconstruction progressed steadily in the years that followed.
By January 2002, about 7.7 lakh houses had been repaired and nearly 60,000 had been reconstructed
.
Reconstructed houses rose to about 1.43 lakh by January 2003 and about 1.87 lakh by January 2004
. The target was about 2.15 lakh houses, so the January 2004 figure was 87 per cent of the target.
Education and Health
By January 2004, all 42,678 primary schoolrooms that had been identified for repair were repaired
. Of the 8,212 destroyed schoolrooms, 7,469 had been reconstructed by then, which is 91 per cent of the total.
The District Civil Hospital at Bhuj was reconstructed with assistance from the Prime Minister's National Relief Fund
. It cost about Rs. 114 crore and used a technology called base isolation, which helps buildings face earthquakes. The hospital was inaugurated on 14 January 2004, completing a key part of the health recovery. Six community health centres, 24 primary health centres, 184 sub-centres and 183 anganwadi centres were also constructed.
Rebuilding Towns
Area Development Authorities were constituted for Bhuj, Anjar, Bhachau and Rapar for town planning and new infrastructure. These Authorities engaged consulting firms to prepare plans, issued building permissions and developed relocation sites.
Town plans were prepared for three of the four towns, which required surveying thousands of plots and settling disputes. Urban infrastructure works included about 403 km of roads, 546 km of water pipelines and 504 km of sewerage.
These works could begin only after development plans; town planning and the selection of contractors were completed. The works also covered 134 municipal buildings, and about 40 per cent had been completed by January 2004.
Livelihoods and Industry
The Government of India and the Government of Gujarat announced tax incentives for new industrial units in Kutch. These incentives included exemptions from excise duty, sales tax and octroi, all of which are taxes on goods.
By March 2004, 151 new industrial projects, with proposed investment of about Rs. 4,785 crore, had been located in Kutch
.
A Lasting Legacy: Institutions for Disaster Management
The recovery also led to lasting reforms, and Gujarat adopted
the State Disaster Management Policy in September 2002
. In 2003, the Gujarat State Disaster Management Act was enacted, which put disaster work on firm legal ground.
The
Gujarat Institute of Disaster Management
was established, and officials and community members were trained. Village-level preparedness teams, called the
Afat Sajjat Senas
, were formed in 484 villages across the State.
In 2002, the State Government took steps to activate the Gram Sabhas, making disaster preparedness a permanent agenda item. The
Sasakawa Award of the United Nations for disaster reduction was conferred in 2003, recognising this work.
In 2004, the
Gold Award of the Commonwealth Association for Public Administration and Management was conferred for innovation in governance
.
Together, these developments preceded the Disaster Management Act, 2005, which applied to the whole country.
Decoding Leadership: Six Lessons from Kutch
Act first, organise as you go.
Relief began within hours, even though landline and mobile networks had failed within the first hour. Clear roles in Bhuj and a same-day meeting of the National Crisis Management Committee kept the response moving.
Build an institution for the mission.
GSDMA was formed within two weeks, with the Chief Minister chairing its Governing Body and a clear mandate. The model was borrowed from Orissa and later given a firm legal basis through the 2003 Act.
Keep people at the centre.
Families rebuilt their own homes, supported by financial assistance, technical guidance and safe designs from the Government. Village Committees and Gram Sabhas also had a voice in the decision to relocate severely damaged villages.
Build fairness into the system.
Open surveys, re-survey requests and an Ombudsman in every district gave families a way to be heard. Staged payments and the independent inspection of about 2.6 lakh houses helped protect the quality of construction.
Review honestly and correct course.
The October 2001 review openly listed problems, from families still in tents to slow urban reconstruction. Senior Secretaries, weekly reviews and a clear deadline then helped the pace of work to increase.
Leave behind capability, not just buildings.
Gujarat gained a policy, a law, a training institute and preparedness teams in 484 villages. These institutions were recognised with the Sasakawa Award in 2003 and a Gold Award in 2004.

title: Leading Through the Storm
subtitle: Governance, Leadership, and Scale in India’s COVID-19 Response
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                16 NOV 2026 10:56AM by PIB Delhi
content:
India’s COVID-19 response shows leadership as a chain of timely decisions, clear mandates and constant course correction. The Government acted before the first case, delegated legal powers and built Empowered Groups that were reshaped as needs changed. The first national serosurvey guided the staged reopening, while private laboratories, hospitals and industry were brought in. Under second-wave pressure, oxygen was allocated to States and vaccination opened to all adults. The effort was sustained until the World Health Organization (WHO) withdrew the emergency status on 5 May 2023. As on 31 December 2025,
97%
of the population aged 12 years and above has received at least one dose of COVID-19 vaccine, while
90%
of this population is fully vaccinated against COVID-19. A total of
22.89 crore
precaution doses have been administered across the country.
A Mission Without a Manual
When an unfamiliar virus reached India, there was no vaccine, no proven treatment and little time. India’s response, from January 2020 to May 2023, unfolded through five phases of preparedness, containment and adaptation. Airport screening, risk assessment and inter-ministerial coordination began before the first case, giving the country a head start. As transmission spread, the response widened to containment, emergency healthcare capacity, oxygen allocation and support for States. Vaccination and phased reopening followed, and the effort lasted until WHO ended the emergency in May 2023. Behind each phase stood leadership choices:
acting early, assigning clear roles, following evidence and adjusting course.
It is a case of leadership as mission, showing how decisions were taken and carried out.
The Challenge
The World Health Organization was notified on 31 December 2019 of pneumonia cases of unknown cause in Wuhan. For India, the early risk was importation through air travel, with preparation time very limited. The Government therefore faced a sequence of connected challenges, each requiring leadership decisions at national scale.
ECRP:
India COVID-19 Emergency Response & Health System Preparedness Package
JMG:
Joint Monitoring Group
Leadership in Action
1. Anticipation: Acting Before the First Case
The Joint Monitoring Group, a standing technical forum of health officials and experts chaired by the Director General of Health Services, met on 8 January 2020 to assess risk and review readiness. Screening of international passengers began on 17 January and extended to 21 airports within a week. This preceded India's first case, reported in Thrissur, Kerala, on 30 January 2020. Seven multidisciplinary Central teams were deputed on 25 January to review airport screening and to assess end to end management of referred suspected cases at the designated hospitals.
The Health Ministry wrote to four other ministries, and the Cabinet Secretariat convened inter-ministerial meetings. A national operations centre, managed by the National Centre for Disease Control, was activated on 8 February. In February 2020, the Government evacuated
645 persons
from Wuhan and placed them in quarantine at two centres.
2. Mandate: Law, Structure and Clear Roles
On 11 March 2020, powers under the Disaster Management Act, 2005 were delegated to the Union Health Secretary. Two days later, States were advised to invoke that Act and the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897, where necessary. On 29 March, eleven Empowered Groups were constituted, each assigned a defined area of responsibility. The areas ranged from the medical plan and testing to supply chains, communication and public grievances. The Cluster Containment Plan of 2 March covered case identification, contact tracing and containment of the surrounding area. A plan for large outbreaks, with a checklist of district-level actions, was shared with States on 4 April. On 28 April, the Union Health Secretary asked all Chief Secretaries to continue essential medical services. A Group of Ministers reviewed progress, and its 14th meeting on 5 May 2020 heard several Empowered Groups. Empowered Groups were led by named senior officials, such as the Union Home Secretary and the Secretary, Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology.
What are the Empowered Groups?
Eleven Empowered Groups were constituted on 29 March 2020, each assigned a defined area, from the medical plan and testing to supply chains and communication. They were consolidated into six in September 2020 and reconstituted into ten in May 2021.
3. Adaptability: A Command Structure That Evolved
The structure was reshaped as needs changed. Eleven groups became six in September 2020; the six were reconstituted into ten on 29 May 2021. The May 2021 reconstitution created separate groups for oxygen, vaccination and testing. Containment also became local, with districts zoned red, orange or green and States asked to strengthen contingency plans. A September 2020 review by the Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister named unlocking with precautions a priority.
4. Evidence: Decisions Guided by Data
The first national serosurvey in May and June 2020 estimated that about 0.73% of the population had been infected. This showed that a large proportion of the population remained susceptible, and reopening proceeded in stages, with workplace guidelines in May and procedures for offices, places of worship, hotels, restaurants and shopping malls in June. In the fourth round of the national serosurvey, 67.6% of the population had antibodies.
What is a Serosurvey?
A serosurvey is a test of blood samples from a cross-section of the population for antibodies, to estimate the share already infected.
Technology and genomics also supported decisions. Close to
9 crore
people had downloaded the Aarogya Setu app by 4 May 2020. Genome sequencing of virus strains from patients across the country had also been initiated by then. INSACOG, the Indian SARS-CoV-2 Consortium on Genomics, was established in December 2020 as the genomic surveillance network. In March 2021, the National Institute of Virology reported the spread of the Delta variant in Maharashtra.
5. Enablement: Bringing Many Hands In
Testing opened to private laboratories on 21 March 2020; by 24 March, 118 laboratories were able to test 12,000 samples daily. Domestic production of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) increased from nil on 1 March to approximately 4.5 lakh coveralls per day by May. HLL Lifecare, a public-sector company, became the single procurement agency, and evaluated bids went daily to the Empowered Group. States were advised to add beds with private hospitals, using PMJAY (Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana) and CGHS (Central Government Health Scheme) rates as reference.
The Group of Ministers also stressed quality control, with random batch sampling of PPEs, masks and ventilators. Empowered Group briefings to the Prime Minister covered partnership with the private sector, NGOs and international organisations. In April 2021, the Prime Minister asked officials to explore using civil society volunteers for non-specialised tasks.
6. Presence: Leading From the Front and in the Field
Reviews chaired by the Prime Minister, Cabinet Secretary and Union Health Minister brought Central ministries and States together. Periodic reviews examined local developments, identified implementation gaps and considered measures needed in affected areas. Multidisciplinary Central teams were deputed to States in 2020 and 2021 to review readiness and containment. Senior Ministry officials were oriented to serve as State nodal officers, with a national training of trainers. Decisions reached States through letters, website advisories and video conferences with States, Union Territories and airport health officers.
Between 20 March and 11 May 2020, the Prime Minister met all Chief Ministers five times virtually. In June 2020, the Prime Minister directed city and district-wise bed planning with States and Union Territories. The June 2020 review also appreciated outstanding work by several States, districts and cities in containing the outbreak. On 27 April 2021, the Prime Minister stressed proper implementation of COVID-19 strategies by agencies in States.
7. Decisiveness: Oxygen and Vaccines Under Pressure
On 15 April 2021, an Empowered Group met on the oxygen situation in twelve States. It mapped supply with industry, regulators and manufacturers, and allocated defined quantities to States for following days.
Communicated allocations rose from 4,880 tonnes on 20 April to 6,593 tonnes on 30 April. States were also asked to set up oxygen plants at hospitals in remote areas, alongside the allocations. The 21 April liberalised strategy permitted flexible pricing and procurement, encouraging manufacturers to expand vaccine production.
Vaccination preparations preceded any vaccine approval, from a task force in April 2020 to a December dry run.
From 1 May
2021
, all adults became eligible for vaccination
, after phased expansion that began with health workers on 16 January 2021. On 27 April 2021, Empowered Groups on oxygen, medical infrastructure and communication briefed the Prime Minister directly.
8. Endurance: Sustaining the Effort
On 8 July 2021, the Cabinet approved Phase II of the India COVID-19 Emergency Response and Health System Preparedness Package (ECRP-II) with an outlay of ₹23,123 crore. The package was directed at district and sub-district capacity and implemented through the National Health Mission. It provided for central hospitals, war rooms and IT systems, genome sequencing, surveillance at 28 points of entry and central procurement of essential supplies. Reported outputs include 663 new laboratories, 697 liquid oxygen tanks, 63 field hospitals and 200 telemedicine hubs.
India crossed one billion doses of vaccination on 21 October 2021. The Union Health Minister asked State and Union Territory Health Ministers on 27 October to start house-to-house vaccination.
The COVID-19 vaccination campaign ‘Har Ghar Dastak’ was launched on 3 November 2021. It aimed at awareness, mobilisation and vaccination of all eligible beneficiaries with the first dose, and of all those due for the second dose, through house-to-house visits in all States and Union Territories.
Vaccination extended to adolescents aged 15 to 18 from 3 January 2022 and 12 to 14 in March 2022. Precaution doses were also offered, including a free drive of 75 days beginning in July 2022. A Revised Surveillance Strategy in June 2022 emphasised early detection, variant tracking and genomic surveillance.
Guidelines on vaccination, home isolation, international arrivals and surveillance were revised periodically from December 2021. In May 2022, India's more than 10 lakh Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) received the WHO Director-General's Global Health Leaders Award. On 5 May 2023, WHO withdrew the Public Health Emergency of International Concern declared on 30 January 2020.
Performance of Vaccination Drive
As on 31 December 2025, 97% of the population aged 12 years and above has received at least one dose of COVID-19 vaccine, while 90% of this population is fully vaccinated against COVID-19. A total of 22.89 crore precaution doses have been administered across the country.
Five Phases at a Glance
PHASE 1
Prepare
Jan to Feb 2020
PHASE 2
Contain
Mar to Apr 2020
PHASE 3
Reopen and prepare
May to Dec 2020
PHASE 4

Jan to Jun 2021
PHASE 5
Build and adapt
Jul 2021 to May 2023

How the Response Was Delivered
Leadership worked through five levels, from apex reviews to districts, with each level reporting upward and acting downward.
Level
Execution
Apex
Periodic reviews by the Prime Minister's Office, with Empowered Groups reporting on progress.
Group of Ministers
Union Health Minister chaired the 14th meeting on 5 May 2020, reviewing containment, supplies, technology and relief.
Empowered Groups
Senior officials led the groups, among them the Union Home Secretary and the Secretary, Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology.
States
Five virtual meetings of the Prime Minister with all Chief Ministers, 20 March to 11 May 2020.
Districts
Red, orange and green zones guided local plans, covering 130, 284 and 319 districts respectively, as on 5 May 2020.
The Takeaway: Leadership as Mission
India’s COVID-19 response was not won by one decision, but by a chain of timely ones. Leaders acted before the first case, gave every task an owner, and let evidence guide each step. They reshaped institutions as the virus changed, and brought industry, laboratories and civil society into one effort. In the second wave, they made hard calls on oxygen and vaccines, then sustained the effort until 2023. The lesson for leaders is clear: anticipate early, empower widely, review often, and adapt without hesitation. That is leadership as mission: a steady purpose, carried out through a plan that never stopped learning.
